title: Using your medicine
intro: Step-by-step guidance on how each form of gender-affirming hormone therapy is used: patches, gels and creams, injections, tablets and implants. It also covers missed doses, storage, and how to get rid of needles and old medicines safely in Australia.

sections.h: Before anything else: your own instructions win
body: Always follow the instructions your prescriber and pharmacist give you, and the Consumer Medicine Information leaflet that comes with your product. Brands differ, and so do people.
If anything below does not match what you were told, what you were told wins. Ask your pharmacist. You do not need an appointment, and you do not need to explain why you are taking it.
sections.note: Nothing here is advice for your particular situation. It is a description of how these products are generally used in Australia.

sections.h: Putting on and changing a patch
body: Estradiol patches are changed twice a week, every three or four days. Most people pick two fixed days, such as Monday and Thursday, and stick to them [1].

The two Australian brands approve different sites, so follow the leaflet for the brand you have. Estradot goes on the abdomen [1]. Estraderm MX goes on the buttock or the lower abdomen [2]. Neither may be applied to the breast or chest tissue. Use clean, dry, hair-free skin, avoid the waistline where a belt or waistband rubs the patch off, and avoid broken or irritated skin. Move to a different spot each time, and leave at least a week before reusing one [3][1][2].

Open the pouch by tearing it. Do not cut it with scissors, which can nick the patch. Peel off the backing without touching the sticky side, press the patch down firmly with your palm for about ten seconds, then run your finger around the edges [3][1].
You can shower and swim with a patch on, though water can lift the edges. If yours lifts, a waterproof dressing over the top can help [3].
Wash your hands before and after handling a patch. Fold an old one in half, sticky sides together, before you bin it. Sticky residue comes off with a little oil or lotion.
list: Choose two set days a week and keep them
Estradot on the abdomen; Estraderm MX on the buttock or lower abdomen; never the breast or chest [1][2]
Press firmly for about 10 seconds and seal the edges
Rotate sites, and leave a week before reusing a spot
Fold used patches in half before binning them
sections.note: If a patch falls off, press it back on, or put on a new one if it will not stick, on a different clean area of skin, and keep your original change days [3][1]. If one comes off repeatedly, tell your pharmacist. The adhesive varies between brands, and that matters more during a shortage, when brands get substituted [4][5].

sections.h: Applying gel, and keeping it off other people
body: Gels and creams are applied once a day, at about the same time, to clean dry skin.

Estradiol gel goes on different areas for each brand, so follow your own leaflet. Sandrena goes on the lower body or thighs, changing sides each day. Estrogel is spread over a large area of the outer arms and shoulders, or the inner thighs [27][28]. Neither goes on the breasts. Keep Estrogel away from the genital area, and keep Sandrena off the face and irritated skin [27][28].
Testogel goes on the upper arms, shoulders or abdomen. Do not put it on the upper chest or the genitals [6][7]. Testavan goes on the upper arm and shoulder only [29].

Testosterone cream (AndroForte 5) is measured with its applicator and goes on the upper body: the torso, abdomen and sides. Massage it in until it is absorbed, about 30 seconds, then cover the area with clothing. Do not shower or swim for at least six hours after applying it. Cream can pass to other people too, so leave six hours between applying it and intimate contact [44].
Wash your hands with soap and water straight after applying, every time [6][7].

Testosterone gel can pass to other people through skin contact. This is not harmless, and it matters most for children, partners and pets that sleep on or against you. Let the gel dry for three to five minutes, then cover the area with clothing. Wash the area with soap and water before close skin contact with anyone [6][7]. Testogel's leaflet says not to shower or bathe for at least one hour after applying (its product information says six hours is better). It also says to leave six hours between applying and intimate contact [6][7]. Testavan's leaflet says to avoid showering or swimming for at least two hours [29]. Follow the leaflet for your own brand.

If gel does get onto someone else's skin, wash that area well with soap and water [6]. Take care with towels, bedding and shared furniture too. Anything that touches the site before it is washed can carry medicine with it.
list: Same time each day, onto clean dry skin
Let it dry fully (about 3–5 minutes), then cover it with clothing [6][7]
Wash your hands straight afterwards
Wash the site before close skin contact with children, partners or pets [6][7]
sections.note: If you are having a blood test to check your level, ask your prescriber when to have it. For estradiol gel, Testogel and testosterone cream, the blood is usually taken just before that day's dose. For estradiol gel, it is best taken from an arm you did not put gel on. For Testavan, it is taken 2 to 4 hours after applying [26].

sections.h: Your long-acting injection: finding the right spot
body: Testosterone undecanoate (Reandron 1000 and other brands) is 1,000 mg of testosterone undecanoate in 4 mL of oil [8]. It is a large, thick injection, and in Australia a doctor, nurse or, in some places, a trained pharmacist gives it. It is not a medicine you inject yourself [9][10].

The recommended site is the side of your hip (the ventrogluteal site), over the gluteus medius muscle. It is not the back of the buttock. SA Health's brochure on long-acting intramuscular injections recommends this site. It is also the site taught in the clinician training package on this site [12][11].

SA Health describes the side of the hip as safer than other sites, with large muscles that absorb medicine well. Injecting into the buttock carries a chance of hitting a large nerve or blood vessel, which sit close to that site [12][11].

The clinician does not guess where it goes. You lie on your side with the upper hip uncovered; only that spot needs to be uncovered, and you can ask for a sheet [11][33]. They put the heel of the opposite hand on the bony knob at the top of your thigh bone. They point their index finger at the bony point at the front of your hip. Then they spread their middle finger back along the top ridge of your hip bone. The injection goes into the middle of the V their fingers make [11][33].

The needle goes straight in at ninety degrees. The 4 mL is pushed in very slowly, over about two minutes [11]. The product information is firm that this injection must go only into muscle, and very slowly. Injecting an oily solution quickly is what causes problems [9][11]. The needle has to be long enough to reach the muscle: the procedure on this site uses a 21-gauge needle 38 mm long, or 50 mm long if your body mass index (BMI) is over 30 [11][33].

The procedure on this site prefers the Z-track technique, and your clinic may use it. Before the needle goes in, the clinician pulls the skin firmly to one side and holds it there while the medicine goes in, waits about 10 seconds, takes the needle out, then lets the skin go. When the skin is let go, the needle track is no longer in a straight line, which helps keep the oil in the muscle [11][33]. It is not part of the product information, so whether it is used follows your clinic's own policy [11].
Afterwards the clinician presses gently on the spot with gauze and puts on a dressing [11].
You may have had this injection in the buttock before. If a clinic now gives it in the side of your hip, that is a planned change, not a mistake.
list: Given by a doctor, nurse or trained pharmacist, into the side of the hip, not the back of the buttock
You lie on your side with the upper hip uncovered
The spot is found from the bony points of your hip, every time
The needle goes in at ninety degrees, and the 4 mL goes in very slowly. Your clinic may also use the Z-track technique
Gentle pressure with gauze and a dressing afterwards

sections.h: What happens at the injection appointment
body: The appointment is short, but you will be asked to stay afterwards. That part matters. The procedure on this site asks you to stay for at least 30 minutes after the injection [11]. The Product Information says to watch for a reaction during and straight after the injection, without giving a fixed time [9].

Before the injection, the clinician checks who you are with at least three details, such as your full name, date of birth and address [11][38]. They ask whether your health has changed since the last injection, including the skin where it was given, and about any side effects since your last dose. They check which side was used last time and use the other side where possible [11][33]. Tell them if you take a medicine that thins the blood, such as warfarin, apixaban or rivaroxaban, or if you have a bleeding disorder. With these, an injection into the muscle can bleed under the skin and leave a large bruise. Testosterone can also make warfarin work more strongly [9][11]. They clean their hands before they touch you and again before the injection [11][37].

You can bring a support person, or ask for a chaperone [11][39], and you can ask the clinician to pause or stop at any time [11]. If you could become pregnant, the clinic may offer you a pregnancy test first; they should explain why, and you can say no [9][11][26].

The reason is a rare reaction called pulmonary oil microembolism, or POME. A small amount of the oil can reach the lungs. It usually shows within minutes, and typically within 30 minutes. The signs are a sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or feeling faint. A very rare allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is also possible [9][11][26].

A 2022 review of 29 studies, covering nearly 8,000 patients, found POME to be rare [13]. Australian standards say most episodes settle on their own within 30 minutes to a few hours, often without treatment [26]. Clinics keep you there because it can be managed and they want to be there if it happens, not because it is likely.
If you feel any of those things, tell staff straight away. Do not wait to see if it passes, and do not walk out to the car park. After you leave, ring 000 if any of these happen [11].
Afterwards the site can ache for a day or two. Walking about helps, and a warm pack and simple pain relief are fine if your pharmacist says they suit you.

The usual schedule is a second dose about six weeks after the first (your prescriber decides), then one every 10 to 14 weeks [9][11]. Book the next one before you leave. That one habit prevents most gaps.

If your clinic is new to this injection, there is a free training package for health professionals on the [testosterone undecanoate page](#/medicines/testosterone-undecanoate#sec-med-9). It has a procedure and training guide (covering the ventrogluteal site, slow injection and the wait afterwards), a competency checklist and an adverse event form. You are welcome to download it and take it with you.
list: Before the injection: questions about any changes or side effects since your last dose, and the other side used where possible
Expect to be at the clinic for a while after the injection, not just for it
Stay for at least 30 minutes; the clinic will have emergency equipment ready
Tell staff straight away about a sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or faintness
Some ache at the site for a day or two is normal
Book the next appointment before you leave: it is usually 10 to 14 weeks away
sections.note: Sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or feeling faint in the minutes after this injection are the symptoms to report on the spot. They are uncommon and they are treatable, and staff would far rather hear about it than not [9][13][11].

body: Many trans people inject testosterone themselves. In Australia that almost always means one of the shorter-acting esters: testosterone enantate (Primoteston Depot) or Sustanon. These are supplied on a private prescription [14][10].

The long-acting undecanoate injection is the exception. Australian general practice guidance states plainly that self-administration is not recommended, and that giving it under the skin rather than into muscle can cause a painful lump [10].

Intramuscular means into the muscle: a longer needle, straight in at ninety degrees. Subcutaneous means into the fat just under the skin, with a shorter, finer needle, and medicine there is taken up more slowly.

Australian prescribing guides describe the esters being given intramuscularly, and note that many people learn to do it themselves [15][10]. Some people and some prescribers use subcutaneous injection instead, but that is a decision for your own prescriber. Only inject under the skin if you have specifically been told to.

Before you do any of this at home, two things need to happen. Someone trained has to teach you in person and watch you do it at least once. TransHub puts it the same way: injections are given by a medical practitioner, or by you or a friend who has been shown how [14]. And you should leave with a written plan: the product, the dose, the route, the site, how often, and who to ring if something does not look right.

Tell your prescriber and the person who trains you if you take a medicine that thins the blood, such as warfarin, or if you have a bleeding disorder. Testosterone can make warfarin-type medicines work more strongly, so your blood clotting may need closer checks [40][41].
list: Get taught in person, and show the person teaching you that you can do it before you do it alone [14]
Ask for the plan in writing: product, dose, route, site, how often, and who to call
Ask them to choose your needle and syringe sizes and write those down too; needle length in particular depends on your body
Get a script or a supply arrangement for needles, syringes and a sharps container at the same time

sections.h: Doing the injection, and what to watch for
body: This part is for injections you give yourself at home, such as short-acting testosterone; the long-acting injection is always given at a clinic. Wash your hands with soap and water, or use alcohol-based hand rub, and set out everything you need before you open anything [37]. Use the sizes your prescriber or trainer chose for you. Their instruction wins over anything on this page.

1. Check the medicine: right product, right strength, in date, and the oil clear rather than cloudy or full of particles. Check that your last injection site has settled, and note any side effects since your last dose to tell your prescriber.
2. Draw up. A glass ampoule snaps open; a rubber-topped vial gets wiped with an alcohol swab first. Draw slowly, because thick oil takes its time.
3. Swap needles. Take the drawing-up needle off and put a fresh injecting needle on. A new needle is sharper and has no oil on the outside, so it hurts less [16].
4. Clear the air. Hold the syringe needle-up, tap until the bubbles rise, and press the plunger gently until they are gone and you are on your dose mark [16].
5. Clean the site with an alcohol swab and let it dry properly. Injecting through wet alcohol is what makes it sting.

6. Insert. Intramuscular is straight in at ninety degrees. Subcutaneous is shallower: pinch up a fold of skin if you are lean. For an injection into the muscle, the person who trains you may teach you the Z-track technique: pull the skin firmly to one side before the needle goes in, and hold it there until the needle is out [33].
7. Inject slowly and steadily. Oil needs time to move, and pushing hard causes most of the soreness afterwards.

8. If you are using the Z-track technique, keep holding the skin to the side, wait about 10 seconds, take the needle out, then let go of the skin. Otherwise, take the needle out. Then press gently with clean gauze and cover it [33].
9. Drop the whole syringe and needle straight into the sharps container, without recapping.

Rotate your sites so no patch of skin is used twice in a row [16]. Subcutaneous injections generally go into the stomach, keeping clear of the belly button, or the thigh [16]. For intramuscular injections at home, overseas guidance gives the outer thigh as the usual site [16], and Canberra Health Services' intramuscular injection procedure lists the outer thigh as an intramuscular site [33]. Australian injection guidance no longer treats the buttock as a preferred site, because of how close it sits to the sciatic nerve and large blood vessels [17]. Use the sites the person who trains you shows you.
A bit of redness, some soreness, a small firm lump that softens over a day or two, and occasionally a bead of blood are all ordinary.
What is not ordinary: redness spreading or streaking away from the site, pain getting worse rather than better, pus, new blisters, or a fever. Any of those, get it looked at the same day [18].
If you get hormones without a prescription, [Using hormones without a prescription](#/diy-hormones#sec-diy-hormones-6) explains where to get clean needles and syringes.
list: Ask your prescriber or the person who trains you which syringe, drawing-up needle and injecting needle to use, and write it down [16]
Alcohol swabs, clean gauze or cotton, and a plastic bandage
A proper sharps container, within reach before you start
sections.note: If you are ever unsure part-way through, stop and ring the clinic or your pharmacist. Nobody minds the question, and it is a much better outcome than guessing.

body: Most tablets are swallowed with water at about the same time each day. Link it to something you do every day, such as brushing your teeth or putting the kettle on, rather than relying on memory.

Some prescribers direct estradiol tablets to be taken sublingually, dissolved under the tongue or between the cheek and gum [19]. That changes how fast the medicine gets in and how blood levels rise and fall, which affects blood test results, so only do it if you have been told to [26].
Micronised progesterone capsules are usually taken at night [15][26].
Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it can make you pass more urine [15]. Its leaflet says to take it at the same time each day [30]; ask your pharmacist whether earlier in the day would suit you.
If you use a dose administration aid (a weekly blister pack made up by your pharmacy), ask whether your hormone medicines can be packed in it. Most tablets can.
Implants are small pellets placed under the skin during a short procedure with local anaesthetic, releasing hormone slowly over months.

TransHub describes estradiol pellets being inserted in a procedure of about fifteen minutes, and replaced every six to twenty-four months depending on how you respond [19]. Testosterone pellets are used by a small number of people, and can only be made by a compounding pharmacy [14]. Neither is a registered, PBS-subsidised product in Australia, so both are paid for privately [14][19].

GnRH analogues used for puberty suppression are also given in a clinic, as an implant or a long-acting injection. Goserelin (Zoladex) is a small implant placed under the skin. Australian standards for young people list the 10.8 mg implant, about every 10 to 12 weeks [42]. Leuprorelin is a depot injection. Eligard strengths last one, three, four or six months [43], and the Australian standards list leuprorelin 22.5 mg or 30 mg every three to four months [42]. Each product's schedule is on the [GnRH analogues page](#/medicines/gnrh-analogues).
Aftercare is simple: keep the site clean and dry for a day or two, and expect some bruising. Contact the clinic if it becomes red, hot, painful or starts to discharge [18].

For daily medicines, leaflets usually say to take a missed dose when you remember. If it is nearly time for the next one, skip the missed dose and carry on. Never take a double dose to catch up [29][30].
For patches, put a new one on as soon as you notice and keep your normal change days [3].
For a missed injection appointment, ring the clinic and rebook rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.
Missing one dose is not an emergency. Missing them repeatedly is worth mentioning, without embarrassment. The fix is usually a different form, a different schedule, or a reminder that works.

If you are ever about to run out because of cost, a shortage, or an appointment you cannot get, talk to your pharmacist before you stop. Hormone therapy is usually meant to be long term. If your ovaries or testes have been removed, your body needs hormone therapy [26]. International guidance says established hormone therapy should be continued, not interrupted, unless there is a medical reason to stop [20].
sections.note: This is general guidance only. Some products have specific instructions, so check the leaflet in your pack or ask your pharmacist.

sections.h: Storing your medicine safely at home
body: Most of these medicines are stored below 25 degrees, in a cool dry place, away from direct sunlight. Do not keep them in the bathroom or in a car [1][7].
Patches stay in their sealed pouches until you use them; gels and creams keep their caps on and stay upright; ampoules and vials stay in their carton, away from light.

A few have a time limit once dispensed or opened: Estalis patches keep for up to one month below 25°C after the pharmacy hands them over, and a Testavan pump for 60 days after it is first opened. Each medicine page gives its brand's rules [31][32].
Keep everything out of reach of children. Testosterone gel in particular should be stored where a child cannot get to it [7].
Check the expiry date when you pick up a new supply, especially if shortages have you keeping a buffer at home. Your pharmacist can confirm the storage rules for your brand.

sections.h: Disposing of needles and leftover medicine
body: Used needles and syringes are sharps, and they never go in a household bin. Put them straight into a sharps container that meets the Australian standard, or at least a rigid, puncture-proof container with a secure screw top. Soft drink bottles, glass jars and cans are not safe. Pharmacies sell them [21][22].

If someone else is pricked by a needle you have used, they should let the wound bleed, wash it with soap and water and rinse well, then cover it with a waterproof dressing [34]. If your blood splashes into someone's eyes, they should take out any contact lenses and rinse the eyes with water [34][35]. Then they should get medical advice straight away: a doctor decides whether treatment is needed to prevent hepatitis B or HIV, and it works best when given early [34][36].

When the container is full, take it to a disposal point: a public sharps bin, or a pharmacy, medical centre or hospital that accepts them. Councils provide many of the public bins, and requirements differ between states [21][22]. In South Australia, the Alcohol and Drug Information Service on 1300 131 340 will tell you your nearest sharps disposal outlet [23].

Unused or expired medicines, such as tablets, patches, gels and leftover ampoules, go back to any community pharmacy under the national Return of Unwanted Medicines program. Every PBS-approved pharmacy has a RUM bin, it is free, and you do not need to explain anything [24].

Hand them in rather than putting them in the rubbish or flushing them: the TGA advises pharmacy return precisely because domestic bins and sinks are dangerous to other people and harmful to the environment [25].
list: Sharps container: rigid, puncture-proof, screw top, kept out of reach
Full container goes to a public sharps bin, pharmacy, medical centre or hospital
Someone else pricked by your used needle: let it bleed, wash it, cover it, and get medical advice straight away [34]
In South Australia, ring 1300 131 340 for your nearest disposal point
Old medicines: hand them in at any pharmacy, free of charge

sections.h: Dose and symptom logs to print
body: A log helps you keep track of each dose, patch change or injection, and any symptoms, to bring to your appointments.
